property_summary: For any interfaceId, the reference contract's supportsInterface(interfaceId) returns true when interfaceId equals type(IAccessControl).interfaceId (i.e. it reports support for IAccessControl), whereas the mutant always returns false and thus fails to report IAccessControl support for that interfaceId.

For every bytes4 iface id, the reference C returns true from supportsInterface(iface) whenever iface == type(IAccessControl).interfaceId (it reports support for IAccessControl); the mutant always returns false and therefore will return false for that specific iface id.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, the reference contract returns true from supportsInterface(interfaceId) exactly when interfaceId == type(IAccessControl).interfaceId (i.e. it reports support for IAccessControl), whereas the mutant always returns false and thus will return false for that specific interfaceId — so the property: calling supportsInterface(id) must return true when id == type(IAccessControl).interfaceId; the mutant violates this for that id.

For any bytes4 iface, the reference C returns true from supportsInterface(iface) when iface == type(IAccessControl).interfaceId, while the mutant that always returns false will return false for that specific iface value (so the property: supportsInterface(ia) == true when ia == type(IAccessControl).interfaceId).

For every bytes4 iface id, the reference contract reports support for IAccessControl (supportsInterface(type(IAccessControl).interfaceId) == true); the mutant that always returns false will return false for that interface id, so the property is violated for that input.

For every interfaceId input, the reference contract reports true for supportsInterface(interfaceId) whenever interfaceId equals IERC165 or IAccessControl (i.e., it returns true for IAccessControl), whereas the mutant reports true only for IERC165 and therefore will return false for interfaceId == type(IAccessControl).interfaceId for some input.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, the reference C returns true from supportsInterface(interfaceId) whenever interfaceId equals type(IAccessControl).interfaceId (in addition to IERC165), whereas the mutant returns false for that interfaceId, so there exists some interfaceId (namely type(IAccessControl).interfaceId) for which the reference returns true and the mutant returns false.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, the correct contract returns true from supportsInterface(interfaceId) whenever interfaceId == type(IAccessControl).interfaceId (in addition to IERC165); the mutant reports support only for IERC165 and thus will return false for interfaceId == type(IAccessControl).interfaceId.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) returns true when interfaceId equals type(IAccessControl).interfaceId (in addition to IERC165); the mutant reports support only for IERC165 and therefore will return false for that interfaceId.

For all 4-byte interfaceId inputs, the reference C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) returns true for IERC165 and for IAccessControl (i.e. returns true when interfaceId == type(IAccessControl).interfaceId), whereas the mutant returns true only for IERC165 — so there exist interfaceId values (notably type(IAccessControl).interfaceId) where reference yields true and mutant yields false.

For every interfaceId input, the correct contract reports support for IERC165 (supportsInterface(type(IERC165).interfaceId) == true), whereas the mutant that only reports IAccessControl will return false for IERC165's interface id.

For every 4-byte interfaceId input, the reference contract C reports support for IERC165 (supportsInterface(type(IERC165).interfaceId) == true) whenever the input equals IERC165's id, while the mutant that only returns true for IAccessControl will return false for IERC165's id — so there exists an interfaceId (specifically type(IERC165).interfaceId) for which the mutant differs; the test fuzzes an interfaceId and asserts that if the input equals IERC165's id then supportsInterface returns true.

For every interfaceId input, the correct contract C always returns true when asked about IERC165's interfaceId (it supports IERC165), whereas the mutant that only reports IAccessControl will return false for IERC165's id — so for some fuzzed interfaceId equal to type(IERC165).interfaceId the mutant and reference differ.

For every 4-byte interfaceId input, the reference C's supportsInterface never reverts and in particular returns true for IERC165's interface id; the mutant returns false for IERC165's id — so the property: calling supportsInterface(type(IERC165).interfaceId) returns true must hold for the reference but is violated by the mutant.

For every 4-byte interfaceId, calling supportsInterface(interfaceId) on the correct contract never reverts and in particular returns true when interfaceId equals type(IERC165).interfaceId; the mutant that only reports IAccessControl returns false for IERC165's id, so there exist inputs for which the return differs.

For every (role, account) the reference contract returns hasRole(role, account) == _roles[role].members[account] (i.e., calling hasRole reflects stored membership); the mutant negates that result and thus for some inputs the returned boolean differs (true vs false).

For any role and account, the reference contract returns hasRole(role, account) equal to the stored membership (i.e. a call to hasRole reflects the actual stored membership); the mutant negates that boolean so for some (role,account) the returned value differs.

For any role and account, calling hasRole(role, account) on the correct contract returns whether that account is currently a member (true iff stored membership is true); the mutant negates that result and thus for some fuzzed role/account pairs the returned boolean differs.

For any role and account, hasRole(role, account) on the correct contract always equals the stored membership (i.e. returns true iff the account was granted the role), while the mutant negates that result and thus for some fuzzed role/account pairs the returned boolean differs; the test asserts that calling hasRole on a freshly-constructed timelock returns true for the contract itself for the TIMELOCK_ADMIN_ROLE (which the constructor always sets), a property the mutant will break for that account/role.

For any role R and account A, if the contract's constructor grants a role to an account then hasRole(R,A) returns true on the reference; the mutant negates hasRole so there exist role/account pairs (e.g. TIMELOCK_ADMIN_ROLE and address(this)) for which the reference returns true but the mutant returns false.

For any role and account, the real contract's hasRole(role, account) returns the stored membership (i.e., it can be false for some inputs), whereas the mutant always returns true — so the invariant is: there exists at least one (role, account) for which hasRole may be false in the reference but the mutant returns true (the mutant violates that membership-reflecting property).

For every role/account pair, the reference contract's hasRole returns whether that account is recorded as a member (so it can be false for some inputs), whereas the mutant always returns true; thus the property: there exist role/account fuzz inputs for which hasRole(...) in the reference can be false — the bug (always true) will disagree for those inputs.

For any role/account pair, calling hasRole(role, account) on the correct contract returns whether that account was granted that role (can be false for many inputs); the mutant always returns true, so there exist fuzzed role/account inputs where correct.hasRole(...) is false but mutant.hasRole(...) is true.

For any role and account the reference contract's hasRole(role, account) returns whether that account is recorded as a member (so calling hasRole may return false for some role/account pairs); the mutant always returns true, so there exist fuzzed (role,account) inputs where reference.hasRole(...) is false but mutant.hasRole(...) would be true.

For any role and account, calling hasRole(role, account) on the correct contract reflects stored membership (can be false) — specifically there exist role/account inputs for which the reference's hasRole returns false but the mutant's always-true implementation would return true.

For any role and account, the reference contract's hasRole(role, account) returns whether that account was granted the role (true when previously granted, false otherwise); the mutant always returns false, so there exist inputs (a role and an account that was granted that role) where the mutant's hasRole differs.

For every role/account pair, hasRole(role, account) in the correct contract returns true if that account was previously granted the role via _setupRole (or other grant) and false otherwise; the mutant always returns false so there exist fuzzed role/account inputs (an account that was set up as a proposer/executor/admin in the constructor) where the mutant's hasRole deviates from the reference.
